text: Gluing strings together sounds like it should be the same everywhere, but it's actually one of the sharpest edges between dialects. Today we're comparing T-SQL's plus operator, Oracle and PostgreSQL's double-pipe, and MySQL's insistence on a function — plus a real trap waiting for anyone who assumes plus just works.

In T-SQL, plus concatenates strings just fine — first name, space, middle name, space, last name. But here's the gotcha: if middle name is NULL, the entire result comes back NULL, not just missing the middle part. One NULL operand poisons the whole expression. CONCAT fixes that, because it treats a NULL as an empty string instead.

Oracle and PostgreSQL both skip plus entirely and use the double-pipe operator — the actual ANSI SQL standard for concatenation. First name, double-pipe, space, double-pipe, last name reads almost like a sentence once you're used to it, and it's identical on both platforms.

Now the real trap. On MySQL, plus is pure arithmetic addition — it is never string concatenation. Write first name plus last name expecting a joined name, and MySQL either throws an error or silently coerces the strings toward zero, producing garbage. There is no plus-based concatenation on MySQL at all. CONCAT of first name, comma, space, comma, last name is the only correct way to do it.

The good news: CONCAT as a function exists on every single one of these platforms — SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL all support it, and it's generally friendlier about NULLs than the native operators. When you're not sure which dialect you're writing for, CONCAT is the safest default. Next lesson: how each platform quotes identifiers — brackets, double quotes, and backticks.
